**Where we are ahead:** the request path is built in — body, typed body, query, typed query and path-param middleware answering an aggregated 400 (or RFC 9457 problem details from the core), which the struct validators leave to the framework; **JSON DoS caps** (depth, array size, members, nodes) enforced by a token scan before the tree exists; a streaming path that validates and decodes in one tokenization into a fixed per-request buffer (~1.5x the body); JSON Schema **export** (`writeJsonSchema`, `writeJsonSchemaFor`); pydantic-style one-error-per-wrong-type aggregation. **Where we are behind:** `pattern` is literal/prefix/suffix/charset only (no regex; the catalog's adopt-list names `mnemnion/mvzr`, so this is not a module gap but is a validator gap -- a caller-supplied `Pattern.matcher` covers it); the go-playground tag count (~170) is NOT matched one-for-one: 34 formats now (the ones a typical user reaches for -- `email`, `url`/`http_url`, `uuid3/4/5`, `base64*`, `hex`, `e164`, `alpha*`, `numeric`, `ascii`, `lowercase`/`uppercase`, `jwt`, `semver`, `cidr`, `mac`, `ip*`, `hostname`, dates -- are there; colours, ISBN/ISSN, SSN, BIC, crypto addresses, `fqdn`, `dns_rfc1035_label`, `latitude`/`longitude`, `html`, `urn_rfc2141`, `datauri`, locale/country/currency codes and the rest are not), no `excluded_*` / `*_with_all` / `*_without_all` / `skip_unless` variants, no `eqcsfield`-style cross-STRUCT paths (a cross rule names a sibling in the same object), no `isdefault`, tag-string parsing (rules are Zig values), custom type functions or translations; cross-field comparisons treat arrays and objects as never equal (go compares lengths); bounds are f64 (an integer value is held to one exactly since 2026-10-24, and integers compare exactly in cross-field comparisons, past i64 too).

## Design & invariants
Three tiers: a pure `Rule`-set validator core (no HTTP) → the typed style `parseInto(T, gpa, body)`
(comptime-reflected schema from struct `T`: optionals → nullable, defaults → not-required, int
bit-width → bounds, enums → `one_of`) plus a runtime-schema style `validateJson`/`validateValue` over
`std.json.Value` → `Body`/`TypedBody(T)`/`Query`/`PathParams` middleware for `router`. Never
fail-fast: every failure is aggregated into the `Report`; a wrong-typed field gets exactly one
`<kind>_type` error (no constraint noise) and other fields keep reporting (pydantic behavior). JSON
DoS caps (`Limits`): a fail-fast streaming token scan (`std.json.Scanner`) enforces `max_depth` (32),
`max_array_elements` (10,000), `max_object_members` (1,000) and `max_total_nodes` (1,000,000) *before*
the document is materialized into a `std.json.Value` tree — a cheap-to-send, expensive-to-parse
payload (deep nesting, huge arrays/objects) is rejected before it can blow up memory/CPU; a breach
yields a clean `too_deep`/`array_too_large`/`too_many_fields`/`too_many_nodes` error, never a panic or
an OOM. Allocation: one arena per validation run, owned by the returned `Report` (`deinit` frees
everything); codes are static strings, composed paths/messages live in the arena, simple paths borrow
`Rule.field` — the schema must outlive the Report. Middleware state is immutable after init, shared
across connection threads (reentrant); success data flows to handlers via a magic-tagged, stackable
`ctx.data` slot chain (`Query` + `Body` compose on one route). Format validators are pure: no
allocation, never panic on any byte sequence. Clean-room; design references pydantic v2 (error shape
+ code vocabulary), JSON Schema draft 2020-12 (keyword semantics + format vocabulary), and
go-playground/validator (struct-tag ergonomics) — behavior/format only, no source copied — see NOTICE.

**Typed query** (`parseQueryLeaky`, 2026-09-28, qap M11.7): a query string decoded into struct `T`
under `rulesFor(T)` + `T.validate_rules` (a `pub` decl: Zig 0.17 `@hasDecl` ignores private ones), with `validateQuery`'s decoding and coercion (lenient
percent-decoding, first duplicate wins, unknown keys ignored). Fields are what one query value can
spell (bool, ints, floats, enums, `[]const u8`, `[N]u8`, `?U` of those; else a compile error); a
field is optional when it has a default. One walk over the query, keys compared as they decode
(no allocation per key); strings borrowed from the query when they needed no decoding.

**Streaming path** (`parseIntoLeaky`, `validateJsonStreaming`, 2026-09-22): the same rules without
the `std.json.Value` tree, for servers that decode into a fixed per-request buffer. The tree is 30–60×
the body (FBA minimum for `parseIntoLimited`: 16.5 KiB body → 955 KiB); the streaming path needs
~1.5× the body + ~2 KiB (same body → 25 KiB). One pass over `std.json.Scanner` tokens: a scalar
becomes a one-node `Value` and goes through the SAME `checkRule` (one implementation of the type gate,
constraints and messages); containers are walked in place (`required` settled at object end,
`min_len`/`max_len` at array end); a container whose rule has `custom` is materialized — that subtree
only — and checked by the tree code; error paths are stack-frame chains rendered only when an error
is recorded; both typed rule sets (derived + `T.validate_rules`) are walked together and
deduplicated as in the tree path. The walker is push-shaped (an explicit frame stack, fed one whole
token at a time), so for a typed body `std.json.parseFromTokenSourceLeaky(T)` pulls the tokens
through a tap that feeds each to the walker, which checks the structural limits on the way too:
**one tokenization** where there used to be three (limit pre-scan, walk, decode). A document the
decoder refuses, or the walker stops (duplicate key, a limit), is answered by the multi-pass path
instead -- pre-scan, walk, `parseFromSliceLeaky` -- so an invalid document gets exactly the report
and precedence it always had. Strings are borrowed from the body. Differences by design: errors in document order (tree: schema order), and a
different subset past `max_errors`. Equality of the error SET and of decoded values is pinned by a
differential fuzz target against the tree path.

**Compiled typed path** (2026-10-24, `parseCompiled`): in front of `parseOnePass`, for every `T`
whose shape and rules allow it (`compiles`: scalars, structs, slices, optionals of them; no `cross`
rule, no `custom` on a container, every rule naming a member `T` has). The walker interprets —
each token goes through `Walker.feed`, keys are matched against both rule sets at run time,
`checkRule` reads rules as data. For a typed body all of that is known at compile time, so this is
a decoder generated from `T` and both rule sets: it drives the scanner itself, decodes every
scalar with std's own `innerParse` (through a one-token source, so values are std's by
construction), and at each value runs exactly the walker's checks in the walker's order, with
`checkRule` inlined on a comptime rule. Reporting is the walker's (`use`, `path`, `gate`,
`finish`), so errors, their order, the cap and the second set's deduplication are the same. It
answers only what it can answer exactly as `parseOnePass` would; a syntax or decode error, a
limit, a duplicate key at any depth, an escaped key (also inside a skipped member),
trailing data, or a value of a shape the type cannot hold makes it give up, and the old paths
answer. The `compiled` fuzz harness requires the identical answer — equal values, or the same
errors in the same order — on every document it answers (`expectCompiledAgrees`).
Measured (scratch harness, `perf stat` min of 5, net of the decode twin, per 16 bodies):
`nested` 357k → 110k cycles (848k → 210k instructions), `invalid` 56k → 26k, `small` 49k → 15k,
`formats` 47k → 16k. Profile before: the walker was ~590 instructions per token (key matching by
`mem.eql` over both rule sets, two out-of-line `checkRule` calls per scalar, frame bookkeeping).

**Cross-field rules** (2026-10-11, `Rule.cross`; parity -- go-playground `eqfield`, `nefield`, `gtfield`,
`gtefield`, `ltfield`, `ltefield`, `required_if`, `required_unless`, `required_with`, `required_without`,
baked_in.go 1372, 1042, 2343, 2299, 2571, 2527, 2120, 2160, 2219, 2264). One implementation (`checkCross`)
for both paths: the tree hands it the object's members, the streaming `Walker` the scalars it captured while
the object went by (`Frame.caps`: only the members some rule's `cross` names, strings copied because the
token is freed after `feed`; a container is recorded as such), and it runs when the object is complete, beside
`required`. Names: codes `field_mismatch` (eq), `field_equal` (ne), `greater_than_field`,
`greater_than_equal_field`, `less_than_field`, `less_than_equal_field`; the presence ops report `missing`.
"Present" is key presence (an explicit `null` is present, as for `required`); go tests the Go zero value, which
JSON cannot tell from absence -- the one named semantic difference. Comparison ops skip a null and a field that
failed its own type gate (one error per field, no noise); a missing sibling fails `eq` and the orderings and
passes `ne` (go: `!ok`). Numbers compare by value (two integers exactly), two date-times / two dates
chronologically (go compares `time.Time`), other strings for `eq` by text and for the orderings by byte length
(go compares `len`). `required_if` needs every entry, `required_unless` any exemption, `required_with` any
present sibling, `required_without` any absent one -- go's own quantifiers. A `custom` predicate on a container
materializes that subtree and the tree code (same `checkCross`) decides inside it. Not exported to JSON Schema:
the comparison ops (2020-12 cannot compare two members); `required_with` is `dependentRequired`, the other
presence ops `allOf` items.

**Array roots** (2026-10-11): a root is one `Rule` (`validateJsonRoot` / `validateJsonRootStreaming`) or a
`[]const T` / `[N]T` typed body (`rootRuleFor`); the walker's root rule is generalized from the implicit
object rule, so an array root costs the same one pass, paths render `[i].field`, the structural `Limits` run
first/along as for objects, and `T.validate_rules` is consulted only for a struct `T`.

## Threat model / out of scope
The JSON structural `Limits` are the security-relevant control here (JSON-DoS mitigation on untrusted
bodies); the byte cap (413) bounds size, the structural scan bounds shape. Explicitly out of scope:
`pattern` is literal/prefix/suffix/charset only — regex is not supported (a tracked future ADOPT
dependency); a top-level JSON array IS describable since 2026-10-11 (`validateJsonRoot`, `[]const T` bodies:
the same `Limits`, errors at `[i].field`); `min`/`max` are f64, so a 54+-bit integer BOUND is the nearest double (an integer value is compared with it exactly) (`parseInto` surfaces an
out-of-range decode as a defensive root-level `invalid` error, never a crash); `uuid` format checks
shape only (the version/variant checks are the separate `uuid3/4/5/7` and `uuid_rfc4122` formats). Duplicate JSON object keys are refused at
every depth, known field or not (`json_invalid`, "DuplicateField") — `std.json`'s default, which
the streaming path reproduces by tracking the keys of every open object (this line said "last wins"
until 2026-09-22; it never did). Not a security boundary beyond the DoS caps — it does
not authenticate, authorize, or sanitize for injection (SQL/HTML); callers still own that.

## Verification
Every rule's code+path, cross-field aggregation, nested paths (`a.b`/`a[i]`), malformed/
empty/truncated JSON → clean `json_invalid` (never a panic), structural-limit rejections at each
bound, typed `parseInto` (derived bounds/enums/defaults/optionals, `validate_rules` merge, JSON-type-
error → pathed-error mapping), query coercion/percent-decoding/duplicate-key handling,
`router.Params` validation, byte-golden 400 error-body JSON; middleware tests over the socket-free
`http.Server.serveStream` (golden 400 + handler-not-invoked proof, valid POST → handler sees parsed
body, typed getter, 413 body cap, stacked Query+Body slot chain); an in-process `router`+`http.Server`
+`http.Client` loopback integration run (invalid POST → 400 with handler never invoked; valid POST →
decoded struct; bad query param → 400). Run: `zig build test-validate`. The rule semantics and the
JSON Schema export are replayed against python-jsonschema and ajv (`schema_oracle_test.zig`, see
Anchoring); regenerate with `tools/schema_oracle.py` (tools/README.md).

**Audit 2026-10-04 (mutation).** 58 schemata mutants over the input guards (`LimitScan`
caps and depth, the error cap and `dedupeFrom`, `checkRule` bounds/`allow_null`/fail-closed
numbers, `.any` constraints, the int gate, every `format` validator's limits, query
coercion and percent-decoding, the streaming `Walker`'s array bounds, duplicate keys,
`required` and dedupe): 54 killed, 4 equivalent, 0 left alive. Equivalent: a second
`partial_number` count in `jsonLimitError` (`Scanner.initCompleteInput` never emits
`partial_number` -- `endOfBufferInNumber` returns a whole `.number` at end of input);
skipping `complete()` after a container closes (keys and values still alternate in pairs,
so member and node counts and therefore every verdict are unchanged); the second-`@` check
in `isEmail` (the domain goes through `isHostname`, which rejects `@`); the `/?#` scan of
the scheme in `isUri` (the scheme loop already admits only ALPHA/DIGIT/`+-.`). Tests added
for the 6 that were real gaps: inclusive lower bounds at their edge on both paths, an
integer beyond i64 failing `int_type`, the exact 253/254-byte hostname edge, query `b=1`
coercing to true.

**2026-10-11 (parity wave).** Cross-field rules are pinned on both paths by `expectBoth` (same errors from
`validateJson` and `validateJsonStreaming`; tests `cross: eq_field ...`, `ne_field`, `gt/gte/lt/lte_field on
numbers`, `ordering strings`, `required_*` x4, the typed `Signup`, the container/null cases, nested + array
items + a materialized object, allocation failures, the schema goldens), array roots by `expectRootBoth`
(`root array: ...` tests, typed `[]const BatchRow` through `expectTypedAgrees`), and each new format by a truth
table citing the baked-in it follows (`format truth table: ...`); the `cross` fuzz harness
(`VALIDATE_FUZZ=<runs> ... --test-filter cross`) runs tree == streaming on random cross-field bodies, also
wrapped as a root array. Anchoring of the new formats: go-playground's regexes/functions read by hand (no
JSON-Schema-Test-Suite file exists for them); NOT yet replayed against a running Go validator.
Performance: `zig build bench-validate` (tools/bench.zig, tools/go_bench) -- see the card.

**Audit 2026-10-24 (wave 8: format oracle, `unique`, numeric `one_of`).** Independent review
(`~/CML/20261024-wave8/validate-review.report.md`): no HIGH; MEDIUM-1 fixed (object members were
combined by a plain sum of hashes under a public key -- a generalized-birthday target that would put
crafted objects in one run of `firstDuplicate`; now hashed in sorted order); LOW-1 fixed (hash and
equality disagreed at the i128 edge: `numberOrder` now orders an integer text past i128 against an
i128-domain value by sign, so `2^127-1` and `2^127` differ, and `-2^127` as an integer and as a float
hash alike); the rest are docs, a tighter oracle class and a table-sanity test. Mutation schemata over
the new code, 87 mutants: 79 killed, 8 equivalent (`colon == 0` redundant with the alphabetic check;
`u@v@[::1]` split at the first `@` -- not RFC 3986, deliberately untested; the `%` zone check redundant
with `netaddr.parseIp`; branch order; sort direction and two loop shapes in `firstDuplicate`; the
object member count implied by the fixed-width member stream). The cost of `firstDuplicate` is pinned
by a test-only comparison counter (`duplicate_comparisons`), which kills the hash-weakening mutants a
correct-answer test cannot see. Card total: 140/154 + 79/87.

The card carries these figures.

- ~~**2026-10-24 (grade-1 wave 6) — P: validation is 1.8–3.5× slower than jprochazk/garde 0.23.0.**~~
  DONE 2026-10-24: the compiled typed path (see *Compiled typed path*); `nested` 3.87× → 1.08×,
  `invalid` 2.02× → 0.89× garde. The gap was the walker interpreting rules per token, not decoding.
- ~~**2026-10-24 (compiled-path review F1) — a `u128`/`i128` member can panic inside std.**~~
  DONE 2026-10-29 (sweep V-5): the typed paths refuse a float-spelled integer that is not integral
  or not below the exact power of two (`i64`/`u64` 2^63/2^64 panicked on the tree path too); 128-bit
  members take only float-spelled values below 2^127 on both entry points (`parseIntoLeaky` decodes
  such a `T` through the checked `Value` route). Integer-spelled values and the derived rules are
  unchanged, so the JSON Schema export is byte-identical.
- **2026-10-24 (review M3) — cross-field comparisons treat two date-time-shaped strings as instants
  whatever the rules' `format`.** `"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"` `eq_field` `"2020-01-01T01:00:00+01:00"` is
  equal, though the text differs; go-playground does this only for `time.Time` fields. Documented
  (README cross-field table); proposed: instants only when either rule has `format = date_time`/`date`.
  Consumer-visible -- owner's call.
- **2026-10-24 (review M4) — `date_time`/`time` accept an offset-less value but export
  `"format":"date-time"`**, which RFC 3339 and ajv/python-jsonschema refuse (the suite case "no time
  offset" is skipped), and a leap second at any time of day: the exported schema is stricter than what
  is enforced. The laxer profile is documented (README). Options: RFC 3339 by default plus an explicit
  local profile, or export the profile as an `x-` annotation with no `format`. Consumer-visible --
  owner's call.
- **2026-10-24 (review, LOW)** — typed float fields accept inf/NaN (`1e400` → +inf, query `nan`)
  unless a bound is set, as pydantic's default; error paths are dotted (a field `a.b` reads as nested);
  `Pattern.matcher` is documented as whole-string while its exported `pattern` is a search; `isUri`
  accepts a non-numeric port outside an IP-literal host (`[`/`]` anywhere and `isCased` = ASCII + Latin-1
  fixed 2026-10-24, go format oracle); the default
  `max_total_nodes` (1M) exceeds what the 1 MiB body cap can hold. Recorded, not planned.
Regex-backed `pattern` support is a tracked future ADOPT dependency (README TODO) — not implemented;
literal/prefix/suffix/charset matching is the v1 ceiling.

The middleware (`Body`/`TypedBody`/`Query`/`PathParams`) answers only in the plain
`{"errors":[…]}` shape with `application/json`. An opt-in to answer as RFC 9457
problem details (`writeErrorsProblem`, `application/problem+json`) is deferred until a
`router`-middleware consumer asks — the one consumer that wanted problem+json (qap,
2026-09-22) calls the core directly, not the middleware.

~~`parseIntoLeaky` scans the body twice~~ — DONE 2026-09-26 (qap M7.3), see *Streaming path*:
one tokenization for every document that decodes (`parseOnePass`), the multi-pass path for the
rest (`parseMultiPass`), both pinned against each other on the corpus and in the differential
fuzz target. Measured on a 33-byte two-field body (`perf stat instructions:u`, ReleaseFast,
stable to the instruction): 7,357 → 5,034 instructions per parse, against 2,221 for a bare
`parseFromSliceLeaky` -- the typed layer's cost down from +5.1 k to +2.8 k. It was three
tokenizations, not two: `jsonLimitError`'s pre-scan counted as well. History of the item:
`parseIntoLeaky` scanned the body twice: `streamValidate` walks it with a `std.json.Scanner`,
then `std.json.parseFromSliceLeaky` tokenizes it again to build `T`. Measured by qap
(2026-09-23, a 50-byte two-field body, `perf stat instructions:u`, stable to ±2 instr): the
typed layer costs **+7.6 k user instructions per request** over a hand-written
`parseFromSlice`, of which ~2.8 k are the second `Scanner.next` pass and ~0.85 k
`Stream.walkValue`. Wanted: one pass that checks the rules and fills `T` from the same
tokens (a validating `parseFromTokenSource`), same error codes and document order, still
body-sized memory. Differential test: one-pass vs today's two-pass on the existing corpus.
Scoped 2026-09-25 (qap M7.3, deferred by the consumer): the second tokenization is ~2.8 k of
the 7.6 k, so the ceiling is ~+12.6 % → ~+9 % per request. Recording the tokens in the walk and
replaying them into `parseFromTokenSourceLeaky` is simple but costs ~5× the body (a token per
~3 bytes at ~16 B each) -- past the body-sized budget a fixed per-request buffer has. The real
fix is a push-shaped walker (explicit frame stack instead of recursion) fed by a token-source
wrapper that `std.json`'s decoder pulls through, with the two-pass path kept as the fallback
for a body the decoder rejects mid-way (so the invalid path still reports every error).
~400-600 lines. Revisit when typed JSON dominates a profile.

Why: go-playground's most-cited feature beyond single-field checks; today only a `custom` predicate on the parent object can express it. Effort: small-medium (a rule kind that takes a sibling name). Fits §2.
- ~~**Top-level array bodies**~~ **DONE 2026-10-11** (`validateJsonRoot`, `[]const T`) *(survey 2026-09-30)* — describe and validate a JSON array root (batch endpoints). Effort: small-medium. Fits §2. (Also named in *Threat model / out of scope*.)
- ~~**Regex `pattern`**~~ *(survey 2026-09-30)* — **DONE 2026-09-30 (user decision) as `Pattern.matcher`**: the caller supplies the matcher (`fn (ctx, string) bool`, e.g. a regex library of their choosing) plus the expression source, which this module only exports (`"pattern"` in `writeJsonSchema`) and quotes in the error; still no regex engine in the repo, and no ADOPT dependency taken.
- ~~**More formats**~~ **DONE 2026-10-11** (22 formats; the rest of the ~170 tags is listed under *Where we are behind*) *(survey 2026-09-30)* — `uuid` version/variant checks (the SPEC notes it checks shape only), `url` scheme restrictions (`http_url`), base64/hex, phone-number-like shapes. Effort: small per format; each anchored on the JSON-Schema-Test-Suite where a vector exists. Fits §2.
- ~~**Differential oracle for the go-playground formats**~~ **DONE 2026-10-24** (`tools/format_oracle.py`, `go_format_test.zig`, see Anchoring): 3,289 strings, every difference decided by a named class; it caught `lowercase`/`uppercase` passing titlecase `ǅ` (case mapping now Go's own tables) and `uri` taking a stray `[`/`]`, and six places where go-playground breaks the RFC its tag names (the `**Ahead:**` line). *(2026-10-11)* — drive the real validator through a Go program over a generated string corpus and freeze its verdicts in a vectors file (as `tools/query_oracle.py` does for the query path), to replace the by-hand reading the 22 new formats are anchored on. Effort: small-medium. Known stricter-than-Go places to confirm: `cidr` prefix with leading zeros, `http_url` with non-ASCII bytes.
- **`excluded_*`, `*_with_all`, `*_without_all`, `skip_unless`** *(2026-10-11)* — the presence-op variants of go-playground not taken in the parity wave (none is reached for as often as the four taken; re-weighed 2026-10-24 for scope `ahead` and left here: each is expressible today as a `custom` predicate on the parent object, and every one needs its own JSON Schema export shape). Effort: small each; same `checkCross` shape.
- ~~**`unique` and `oneof` on numbers**~~ **DONE 2026-10-24** — `Rule.unique` (JSON Schema `uniqueItems`, JSON equality, O(n log n) via a SipHash128 structural hash, streaming paths materialize the array) and `one_of` on `.int`/`.float` rules compared by value (it was ignored there, while the export listed the entries as strings and so refused every number). Both replayed by python-jsonschema and ajv (four crafted rule sets); `unique` also against a quadratic model (`unique` fuzz harness).
- **Cross-field rules on query/path params** *(2026-10-11)* — `validateQuery` / `validateParams` ignore `Rule.cross`. Effort: small, but needs the coerced values of all parameters.

## Status
`gap · any · util · reentrant` + deps: `router`, `http`, `netaddr` — canonical source is
`pub const meta` in src/root.zig.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** src/json_schema_format_test.zig runs the official json-schema-org/JSON-Schema-Test-Suite optional/format files (src/testdata/json-schema-test-suite, 12 formats), which is where the isDuration bug was found. src/schema_oracle_test.zig replays python-jsonschema 4.19.2 and ajv 8.20.0 (`tools/schema_oracle.py`, frozen 2026-10-05, re-taken 2026-10-24): 317 rule sets (17 crafted, 300 generated: every kind, `required`, `allow_null`, bounds, code-point and byte lengths, `one_of`, the four built-in patterns, nested `fields`/`items` two deep), each of which must export exactly the frozen schema, and 2075 documents that `validateJson` and `validateJsonStreaming` must answer as both validators do -- or as a named class decides (f64 bounds past 2^53 -- Python decides, since 2026-10-24; `$` before a final newline left with the `(?![\s\S])` export end, `1e400` as an integer, the byte bounds a schema cannot state, an unpaired surrogate escape), each class pinned to at least one case. src/query_oracle_test.zig replays the text path (`tools/query_oracle.py`, frozen 2026-10-06): 39 query strings whose first value of a field must decode as Python's `parse_qsl`, Go's `net/url` and WHATWG `URLSearchParams` decode it, and 336 values against 12 rules (int with no, small, i64 and u64 bounds; float; bool; string lengths, `one_of`, `charset`) that `validateQuery` must accept or refuse with pydantic 2.13.5's error code -- pydantic in lax mode fed the very bytes the module decodes, Go's strconv/math.big and Python's `int()`/`float()` beside it. Six named classes decide where they split (Go drops a pair with a bad escape or a `;`; WHATWG replaces bytes that are not UTF-8; pydantic strips whitespace around a number and takes `5.0` as an int, Go does not and neither does the module; an integer past 2^53 against an f64 bound, compared exactly), each pinned to at least one case. src/go_format_test.zig replays go-playground/validator v10.30.5 itself on its own formats (`tools/format_oracle.py`, `tools/go_formats`, frozen 2026-10-24): 3,289 strings over the 29 formats go has a tag for (crafted edge cases plus seeded mutations), each answered as `validate.Var(s, tag)` does or as a named class decides, every class deciding at least one case. Six classes are go-playground breaking the RFC its tag names (MAPPED_V4, HOSTNAME_253, EMAIL_LOCAL_64, EMAIL_DOMAIN, HTTP_EMPTY_HOST, DT_OFFSET_24 -- the `**Ahead:**` line); the rest are this module's documented profile (EMAIL_QUOTED, EMAIL_NON_ASCII, URL_RFC3986_CHARS, URI_RELATIVE, URI_RFC3986_CHARS, URI_PCT_HOST, UUID_RFC4122_STRICT, CIDR_PREFIX_ZEROS, DT_PROFILE). `lowercase`/`uppercase` match go exactly: their change-sets are generated from Go's `unicode` package (`tools/go_casetables`). Not anchored, and not wire behaviour: the `rulesFor` mapping from Zig types (reflection no foreign implementation has; its bounds are the types' own), `custom`/`matcher` (code), `format` inside the oracles (left to the suite), and the English message text.

**How it got there.** The anchoring work landed. DONE 76f9d9c: format vocabulary only (rest out of scope), isDuration bug fixed. 2026-10-05: the schema oracle -- the rule semantics and the export judged by two foreign 2020-12 validators. It found four defects, all where the validator was looser than the schema it exports: `.any` with `one_of` or a `literal` accepted any non-string (`5`, `null`, `[]`); an integer literal past i64 was `int_type` while `1e23` passed (and `parseInto` refused every `u64` above 2^63-1); a non-ASCII `charset` compared bytes (`â` passed `¢ü`); `allow_null` with `one_of`/`literal` exported an `enum`/`const` that refuses the null the validator accepts. 2026-10-06: the query oracle -- decoding agreed with all three parsers; coercion had five defects: a NaN passed every bound (`n < min` is false for NaN); an integer past i64 was `int_parsing` (a `u64` query field refused 2^63..2^64-1); `1__0` passed as an int and `0x10`/`0x1p3` as floats (`std.fmt` grammar, refused by pydantic, Python and JSON); bytes that are not UTF-8 passed as a string (`string_unicode` only when a length rule was present). `t`/`f`/`on`/`yes`/`y`/`n`/`off`/`no` were `bool_parsing`; pydantic's vocabulary, a superset of Go's, is taken now.
